text: After the Deluge, also known as The Forty-First Day, is a Symbolist oil painting by English artist George Frederic Watts, first exhibited in an incomplete form as The Sun at St Jude's Church in Whitechapel in 1886 and completed in 1891. The painting depicts a scene from the story of Noah's Flood, showing Noah opening the window of his Ark to see that after forty days of rain the floodwaters have not yet subsided but the rain has stopped. Watts, who was born in 1817 to a London musical instrument manufacturer, developed a lifelong obsession with death following the deaths of his two brothers in 1823 and his mother in 1826. He was apprenticed as a sculptor at age 10 and by his mid-teens earned a living as a portrait painter; he joined the Royal Academy of Arts at 18, though he disliked its methods and attended intermittently. From 1837, he became fully dedicated to painting, and after traveling to Italy in 1843 for four years, he returned to London suffering from melancholia and painted many gloomy works. His skills were widely recognized, and in 1856 he focused on portrait painting, which was highly regarded, leading to his election to the Royal Academy in 1867—the highest honor available to an artist at the time—though he soon became disillusioned with its culture. From 1870, he gained fame as a painter of allegorical and mythical subjects, becoming one of the world’s most respected artists. In 1881, he added a glass-roofed gallery to his home at Little Holland House, which opened to the public and boosted his visibility. Despite his father’s strict evangelical Christianity and his personal dislike of organized religion, Watts had a deep knowledge of the Bible and frequently painted Noah and the Flood, seeing modern society’s prioritization of wealth over moral values as a decline akin to the biblical cleansing of a degenerate world. He believed this societal shift, which he described as "the hypocritical veiling of the daily sacrifice made to this deity," was leading to societal collapse. The painting illustrates the moment when sunlight first becomes visible after 40 days of rain, with a bright sunburst breaking through clouds, a highly stylized seascape where light rays project beyond the canvas. This composition echoes J. M. W. Turner’s 1843 painting Light and Colour (Goethe's Theory) – The Morning after the Deluge – Moses Writing the Book of Genesis, which features a circle of light but includes recognizable human figures, unlike Watts’s abstract approach. Watts’s interest in the sun as a divine symbol stemmed from his acquaintance with Max Müller, who promoted solar theories of mythology. His widow, Mary Seton Watts, wrote that Watts deliberately avoided depicting the Creator directly, stating that he wanted viewers to imagine the Creator’s hand moving through light and heat to re-create, emphasizing the power of light rather than painting a portrait of the sun. Although he had previously painted an orange sun above a flat sea in The Genius of Greek Poetry (1878), which evoked pantheism, After the Deluge was explicitly intended as a monotheistic image, reflecting the magnificence and redemptive mercy of a single, all-powerful God. The completed painting was first exhibited at the New Gallery in 1891, and accompanied by an explanatory note stating: "A transcendent power of light and heat bursts forth to re-create; darkness is chased away; the waters, obedient to the higher law, already disperse into vapoury mists and pass from the face of the earth." Between 1902 and 1906, it was exhibited across the United Kingdom in Cork, Edinburgh, Manchester, Dublin, and at Little Holland House, and in 1904 it was transferred to the newly opened Watts Gallery in Compton, Surrey, shortly before Watts’s death that year. Although Watts did not include After the Deluge in his 1886 donation of his 23 most significant non-portrait works to the nation, it was greatly admired by fellow artists and has been cited as an influence on painters such as Maurice Chabas, Giuseppe Pellizza da Volpedo, and Edvard Munch. Despite its omission from the national collection, it remains in the Watts Gallery’s collection and is recognized as a landscape stripped of materialism, offering a poetic, sublimated vision of nature.
